prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that the improper joinder doctrine requires the removing party to show there is no reasonable basis to predict recovery against the in-state defendant.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fifth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. Defendants cannot carry their heavy burden of showing that Plaintiff has no reasonable basis of recovery against the in-state defendant.**

A defendant may remove a case on diversity grounds only if no properly joined defendant is a citizen of the forum state. The improper joinder doctrine is a narrow exception to the rule of complete diversity. *Smallwood v. Ill. Cent. R.R. Co.*, 385 F.3d 568, 572–73 (5th Cir. 2004) (en banc). The party invoking it must show one of two things. It must show either "actual fraud in the pleading of jurisdictional facts" or an "inability of the plaintiff to establish a cause of action against the non-diverse party in state court." *Id.* at 573 (quoting *Travis v. Irby*, 326 F.3d 644, 646–47 (5th Cir. 2003)). Defendants do not allege fraud in the pleadings. Only the second route is at issue.

The Fifth Circuit has stated the second test this way. The question is "whether the defendant has demonstrated that there is no possibility of recovery by the plaintiff against an in-state defendant, which stated differently means that there is no reasonable basis for the district court to predict that the plaintiff might be able to recover against an in-state defendant." *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573. The possibility of recovery must be reasonable and not merely theoretical. *Id.*; *Campbell v. Stone Ins., Inc.*, 509 F.3d 665, 669 (5th Cir. 2007); *Griggs v. State Farm Lloyds*, 181 F.3d 694, 699–700 (5th Cir. 1999). Because the test asks whether recovery is reasonably possible, a plaintiff need not show that he will probably prevail or even that he is likely to. The question is whether a state court could reasonably find liability on the pleaded facts.

The burden stays with the removing party throughout. That party's burden is "heavy." *Cuevas v. BAC Home Loans Servicing, LP*, 648 F.3d 242, 249 (5th Cir. 2011); *Great Plains Tr. Co. v. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Co.*, 313 F.3d 305, 312 (5th Cir. 2002). The burden is heavy for a reason. Removal jurisdiction raises federalism concerns, so the removal statute is strictly construed and doubts are resolved in favor of remand. *Cuevas*, 648 F.3d at 249; *Hart v. Bayer Corp.*, 199 F.3d 239, 246 (5th Cir. 2000). Courts must also resolve all contested issues of fact and all ambiguities in state law in the plaintiff's favor. *Griggs*, 181 F.3d at 699; *Burden v. Gen. Dynamics Corp.*, 60 F.3d 213, 216 (5th Cir. 1995). A defendant therefore cannot meet its burden by arguing that the state-law claim is doubtful. It must show that the claim has no reasonable basis.

The usual method is a Rule 12(b)(6)-type analysis. The court looks at the allegations of the complaint and asks whether they state a claim against the in-state defendant under state law. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573; *Campbell*, 509 F.3d at 669. The court must apply the federal pleading standard in doing so. *Int'l Energy Ventures Mgmt., L.L.C. v. United Energy Grp., Ltd.*, 818 F.3d 193, 200–08 (5th Cir. 2016). A court may "pierce the pleadings" only in the rare case where a plaintiff has stated a claim but has "misstated or omitted discrete facts that would determine the propriety of joinder." *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573. Even then, the inquiry must be summary and limited. *Id.* at 573–74; *McDonal v. Abbott Labs.*, 408 F.3d 177, 183 (5th Cir. 2005). A court may not use it as a vehicle for a mini-trial on the merits. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 574. Nor may a court use it to decide whether the plaintiff will ultimately succeed. *Davidson v. Ga.-Pac., L.L.C.*, 819 F.3d 758, 765 (5th Cir. 2016).

Applying these principles here, Plaintiff's complaint alleges [facts supporting a claim against the in-state defendant] and identifies the state-law basis for liability. [Insert application, including the elements pleaded and the record support.] Those allegations are enough to establish a reasonable basis for predicting recovery under [state] law. Defendants' contrary arguments rely on contested facts and on disputed points of state law. Both must be resolved in Plaintiff's favor at this stage. *Griggs*, 181 F.3d at 699. Defendants have therefore not carried their heavy burden of showing improper joinder. Because the in-state defendant was properly joined, complete diversity is lacking and the case must be remanded.
